qa.name: Gastrocnemius
qa.origin: Medial head: posterior surface of medial femoral condyle. Lateral head: posterior surface of lateral femoral condyle
qa.insertion: Posterior surface of calcaneus via the calcaneal (Achilles) tendon, shared with soleus
qa.innervation: Tibial nerve (S1, S2); two-joint muscle — crosses knee and ankle
qa.function: Plantarflexes the ankle (powerful); flexes the knee. Two-joint muscle crossing both knee and ankle
qa.opposing_muscle: Tibialis Anterior, EHL, EDL (dorsiflexion); quadriceps (knee flexion vs extension)
qa.clinical_note: Gastrocnemius is one muscle with two heads — Medial and Lateral. Together with Soleus it forms the Triceps Surae, inserting via the Achilles tendon. Gastrocnemius is a two-joint muscle (crosses knee and ankle) while Soleus is a single-joint muscle (ankle only). Gastrocnemius is most active during fast walking and running; Soleus during slow walking and standing. The Silfverskiöld test distinguishes gastrocnemius tightness (equinus corrects with knee flexion) from combined gastrocnemius-soleus tightness (equinus persists with knee flexion). Innervated by the tibial nerve (S1–S2).

qa.name: Gastrocnemius — Medial Head
qa.origin: Posterior surface of the medial femoral condyle and adjacent femoral shaft
qa.insertion: Posterior surface of calcaneus via calcaneal (Achilles) tendon
qa.innervation: Tibial nerve (S1, S2); medial head — larger, extends more distally
qa.function: Plantarflexes the ankle; flexes the knee. Medial head is the larger of the two heads
qa.blood_supply: Medial sural artery (branch of popliteal artery)
qa.clinical_note: The medial head of gastrocnemius is larger and extends further distally than the lateral head. Gastrocnemius is one muscle with two heads sharing a common insertion via the Achilles tendon. The medial gastrocnemius flap is a workhorse in reconstructive surgery — used to cover exposed bone and hardware in proximal tibial wounds. Tennis leg (acute calf pain from sudden plantarflexion against resistance) typically involves a tear at the medial gastrocnemius musculotendinous junction.

qa.name: Gastrocnemius — Lateral Head
qa.origin: Posterior surface of the lateral femoral condyle and adjacent femoral shaft
qa.insertion: Posterior surface of calcaneus via calcaneal (Achilles) tendon
qa.innervation: Tibial nerve (S1, S2); lateral head — smaller, may contain fabella
qa.function: Plantarflexes the ankle; flexes the knee. Lateral head is the smaller of the two heads
qa.blood_supply: Lateral sural artery (branch of popliteal artery)
qa.clinical_note: The lateral head of gastrocnemius is smaller than the medial head. A fabella (sesamoid bone) is found in the lateral head tendon in approximately 25% of people — visible on lateral knee X-ray and occasionally causing posterolateral knee pain (fabella syndrome). Gastrocnemius is one muscle with two heads; both are innervated by the tibial nerve (S1–S2). The two heads form the lower boundaries of the popliteal fossa — medial head forms the inferomedial boundary, lateral head forms the inferolateral boundary.

qa.name: Soleus
qa.origin: Posterior surface of fibular head and upper quarter of fibula; soleal line and middle third of medial border of tibia; fibrous arch between tibia and fibula
qa.insertion: Posterior surface of calcaneus via calcaneal (Achilles) tendon, shared with gastrocnemius
qa.innervation: Tibial nerve (S1, S2); single-joint muscle — ankle only
qa.function: Plantarflexes the ankle; postural muscle — maintains standing posture against forward sway; pumps venous blood from the leg (soleal venous sinuses)
qa.blood_supply: Sural arteries; fibular artery; posterior tibial artery
qa.clinical_note: Soleus lies deep to gastrocnemius and together they form the Triceps Surae. Unlike gastrocnemius it is a single-joint muscle (ankle only) — it continues to plantarflex even with the knee flexed, when gastrocnemius is slack. It contains the soleal venous sinuses — large venous lakes that are a major site of deep vein thrombosis (DVT) formation after surgery or immobility. Soleus is predominantly slow-twitch (Type I) muscle — built for endurance and postural control. The Achilles tendon, shared with gastrocnemius, is the largest and strongest tendon in the body.

qa.name: Plantaris
qa.origin: Lateral supracondylar line of femur and oblique popliteal ligament
qa.insertion: Posterior surface of calcaneus (medial to Achilles tendon)
qa.innervation: Tibial nerve (S1, S2); vestigial muscle with very long slender tendon
qa.function: Weak plantarflexion of the ankle; weak knee flexion; vestigial muscle of minimal functional significance
qa.clinical_note: Plantaris is a vestigial muscle with a very small belly and an extremely long thin tendon (up to 40 cm) — one of the longest tendons in the body. It is absent in approximately 10% of people. Its tendon runs between gastrocnemius and soleus to insert medial to the Achilles tendon. Clinically important because its rupture (plantaris tear) causes sudden sharp posteromedial calf pain, mistaken for a DVT or partial Achilles rupture — treated conservatively. The plantaris tendon is harvested as a graft in tendon repair surgery.
